Wildfire risk to United States cultural resources

Mona M. Farnisa, Benjamin S. Halpern, Caitlin R. Fong · Scientific Reports 16, 21599 (2026) · open access

Which of the nation's historic places stand where wildfire is most likely? This map shows 56,106 places on the National Register of Historic Places, from single houses and bridges to whole historic districts, each coloured by the wildfire burn hazard around it.

  • Search for a place by its name or town
  • Hover over or tap a dot for its details and its National Register record
  • Colour the dots by burn hazard, level of significance or property type

It does not show current fires, fire perimeters, closures or evacuation orders, and a low burn hazard here does not mean a place is safe from fire. Do not use it during an active wildfire. Wildfire risk to United States cultural resources

Burn hazard around 56,106 places on the National Register of Historic Places, in all 50 states. From Farnisa, Halpern & Fong, Scientific Reports (2026).

    Click a group to hide or show itTap a group to hide it

    About this map

    Each dot is one place listed on the National Register of Historic Places, the U.S. list of buildings, districts, structures, sites and objects judged worth preserving. The map shows 56,106 of them in all 50 states (the District of Columbia is not included): the listed places where the land at the place itself has some chance of burning. Places where that chance is zero are left out. Each dot sits at the centre of the place's mapped outline. The map comes from the paper by Mona M. Farnisa, Benjamin S. Halpern and Caitlin R. Fong, Wildfire risk to United States cultural resources, Scientific Reports 16, 21599 (2026), which is open access.

    Not for emergency use

    This map is part of a scientific research project at the National Center for Ecological Analysis and Synthesis (NCEAS), University of California, Santa Barbara, and is shared for information only. It does not show current fires, fire perimeters, closures or evacuation orders, and a low burn hazard does not mean a place is safe from fire. In an emergency, follow instructions from local officials and contact your local emergency management agency; in a life-threatening emergency, call 911.

    Burn hazard

    Burn hazard combines two values of annual burn probability within 500 m of each place: the average and the highest. Each is rescaled from 0 to 1 across all places (the top 1% are capped at 1), and the two are averaged into one score. Places are then grouped by where they fall among all 56,106:

    • Low: the lower half (score ≤ 0.009)
    • Moderate: between the middle and the top tenth (0.009 < score ≤ 0.130)
    • High: the top tenth (score > 0.130)

    Burn probability comes from the USDA Forest Service Wildfire Risk to Communities data (270 m cells). It is a long-run likelihood, not a forecast for this year.

    Level of significance

    Each National Register nomination records whether a place matters to its local community, its state, the nation or, rarely, the world. Where a nomination gives several levels, the map shows national first, then state, then local. 113 places have no level recorded. 1,449 places are also National Historic Landmarks; their cards say so.

    Property type

    • Building: built mainly to shelter people or activities, such as a house, church or barn
    • District: a group of related buildings, sites or structures, such as a historic town centre
    • Structure: built for purposes other than shelter, such as a bridge, dam or lighthouse
    • Site: a place of a significant event or activity, such as a battlefield or archaeological site
    • Object: mainly artistic or small in scale, such as a monument, sculpture or boat

    27 places have no type recorded. The colours on this map match the figures in the paper.
